passages.title: The Prophet rebuked over the blind seeker
passages.tafsir:
## The Prophet ﷺ rebuked over the blind seeker

These ten ayat record one of the most remarkable moments in the Qur'an. A blind Companion interrupted the Prophet ﷺ at a delicate moment, the Prophet ﷺ frowned and turned away from him — and, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it, when the assembly broke up these verses were revealed "to record Allah's dislike for this attitude, and to give directions for future." What binds ayat 1–10 together is a single contrast, drawn twice: the man who "thinks himself self-sufficient" (ayat 5–7) set against the man "who came to you running, and is afraid" (ayat 8–10).

## The story behind the passage

The occasion of revelation is reported by more than one of the scholars of tafsir, as Ibn Kathir notes. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ was in conversation with one of the great leaders of the Quraysh, hoping he would accept Islam. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān names those present: ʿUtbah ibn Rabīʿah, Abū Jahl ibn Hishām, and the Prophet's ﷺ uncle ʿAbbās — who at that time had not yet embraced Islam.

Into this gathering came ʿAbdullāh ibn Umm Maktūm, a blind man who had accepted Islam in its earliest days. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, citing Imam Baghawī (via Mazharī), adds the crucial detail: being blind, he could not see that the Prophet ﷺ was occupied. So he burst into the circle and called out to the Prophet ﷺ repeatedly, urgently begging to be taught — according to Ibn Kathir, asking that the Prophet ﷺ teach him a verse of the Qur'an, and insisting on an immediate answer.

The Prophet ﷺ disliked the interruption. He reasoned that Ibn Umm Maktūm was a committed Muslim who visited him often and could be taught at any time, while the Quraysh chiefs almost never sat to listen — if this conversation broke off, they might be lost to Islam forever. So he frowned at Ibn Umm Maktūm and turned to face the other man. When the assembly broke up, this sūrah was revealed.

Ibn Kathir also records the report of ʿĀ'ishah — narrated by Abū Yaʿlā and Ibn Jarīr — that the passage "was revealed about Ibn Umm Maktūm, the blind man," who came saying "Guide me" while the Prophet ﷺ was with one of the great leaders of the idolaters; the Prophet ﷺ turned to the leader and asked, "Do you think that there is a problem with what I am saying?" and the man said "No." Ibn Kathir adds that at-Tirmidhī recorded this hadith without mentioning ʿĀ'ishah, and that it appears likewise in al-Muwaṭṭa'.

## Why the Prophet ﷺ did what he did — and what Allah taught instead

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is careful to explain that the Prophet's ﷺ action was not carelessness or pride. It was *ijtihād* — a considered judgment based on personal reasoning. Two things weighed in his mind. First, interrupting a gathering out of turn is a breach of etiquette that would normally merit gentle correction. Second, disbelief and *shirk* (associating partners with Allah) are the gravest of all sins, so drawing these chiefs out of them seemed to take priority over the supplementary question a believer was asking. There was, apparently, no religious loss in making a believer wait.

Allah did not confirm this reasoning. The correction turns on a distinction between the *certain* and the *doubtful*. Teaching a genuine seeker like Ibn Umm Maktūm would most certainly benefit him; the benefit of conversing with opponents who disdainfully turn away is shaky and doubtful — and a doubtful thing cannot be preferred over a certain one.

And what of Ibn Umm Maktūm's own breach of etiquette? Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points out that the Qur'an itself supplies his excuse in a single word: "the blind man" (ayah 2). He could not see whom the Prophet ﷺ was with. An excusable person who breaks a rule of conduct unwittingly should not be reprimanded — a principle the wording quietly teaches.

## The astonishing courtesy of the grammar

The opening words carry a subtlety that Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out beautifully. *ʿAbasa* means "he frowned"; *tawallā*, "he turned aside." Since the Prophet ﷺ himself is being addressed, we would expect the second person: "*you* frowned and *you* turned away." Instead, ayat 1–2 speak in the third person — as if the deed were done by someone else — to preserve the honour of the Prophet ﷺ, while still subtly signalling that the act was not befitting his high station.

Then in ayah 3 the address pivots to the second person: "And how can *you* know that he might become pure?" This switch, too, is deliberate. Had Allah never addressed him directly, the Prophet ﷺ might have felt he was being shunned over his conduct — an unbearable pain and grief for him. So, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains, the third person at the start is meant to show him respect, and the second person that follows is meant to honour and console him.

Notice too that ayah 3 — "what could tell you?" — hints at his excuse: it simply had not come to his attention that the Companion's request carried certain benefit while the other conversation's benefit was dubious.

## Two words for two kinds of benefit (ayat 3–4)

The Qur'an holds out two possibilities for Ibn Umm Maktūm: *yazzakkā*, "he might become pure," and *yadhdhakkar*, "he might receive admonition and the reminder benefit him." Ibn Kathir explains the first as attaining purification and cleanliness of soul, and the second as taking admonition and abstaining from the forbidden.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads in the pair two stages of the spiritual path. Purification — cleansing one's inner and outer self — is the station of the righteous. Taking heed of the reminder is the station of the *mubtadi'*, the beginner on the spiritual journey, in whose heart the remembrance of Allah increases His greatness and awe. The two are joined by "or," but they are not mutually exclusive: the sense is that this genuine believer would certainly have gained at least the second benefit — increased remembrance and awe of Allah, the first step toward perfection — and quite possibly both. (Mufti Taqi Usmani notes that *dhikrā* here has been read by some as "remembrance of Allah," per the Ṣiḥāḥ, and by others simply as "the advice.")

Either way, the benefit was guaranteed. That is the whole point of ayah 3's question.

## The two men, side by side (ayat 5–10)

The passage then lays the contrast bare in two matched panels.

**Ayat 5–7:** "As for him who thinks himself self-sufficient — to him you attend; what does it matter to you if he will not become pure?" Maʿārif ul Qurʼān renders the word *istaghnā* as "the one who does not care [about faith]" — the indifferent man. Ibn Kathir paraphrases: "you face the rich person so that perhaps he may be guided... but you are not responsible for him if he does not attain purification." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it directly: you pursue those who turn away, hoping they will somehow become Muslims — yet this is not your responsibility, and if they refuse the faith, no blame falls on you.

**Ayat 8–10:** "But as for him who came to you running, and is afraid — of him you are neglectful." Here is Ibn Umm Maktūm: hurrying to the Prophet ﷺ of his own accord, afraid, seeking — as Ibn Kathir puts it — to be guided by what the Prophet ﷺ would say to him, and finding him "too busy," as Ibn Kathir glosses *talahhā* (ayah 10), diverted toward another.

One man is pursued though indifferent; the other is set aside though yearning. The revelation reverses the scale: receptivity to guidance, not social weight, is what counts.

## The principle the passage establishes

Ibn Kathir draws the enduring rule: here Allah commands His Messenger ﷺ not to single anyone out in conveying the warning, but to warn equally the noble and the weak, the poor and the rich, the master and the slave, men and women, young and old — "then Allah will guide whomever He chooses to a path that is straight."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān frames it as a Qur'anic principle of teaching and preaching. The Prophet ﷺ faced two duties at once: teaching a Muslim seeking to grow, and inviting non-Muslims to the faith. The passage rules that the first takes priority — the education and reform of the Muslims comes before, and must not be delayed for, the effort to win over those outside the faith. Scholars and preachers, it adds, should never handle the doubts of outsiders in ways that sow doubt or grievance among the general body of believers. The Urdu poet Akbar Allahabadi versified the idea: better that outsiders call you ill-mannered than that your own people find you unfaithful.

## Living it

The passage speaks plainly to anyone who teaches, calls to Allah, or simply manages their attention among people:

- **Weigh benefit, not status.** The sincere questioner in front of you carries certain benefit; the impressive audience that "might come around" carries only doubtful benefit. The certain is never sacrificed for the doubtful.
- **Guidance is Allah's; conveying is yours.** Ayah 7 releases the caller from anxiety over outcomes: "What does it matter to you if he will not become pure?" You answer for the effort, not the result.
- **Excuse the excusable.** Ibn Umm Maktūm broke the etiquette of the gathering, but unknowingly — and the Qur'an named him only "the blind man" to enshrine his excuse. One who errs unwittingly is not to be met with aversion.
- **Note whom Allah defended.** The person these verses were revealed about was a blind man — the "weak man," as Ibn Kathir's heading calls him — an early believer sincerely begging to be taught. Warning and teaching, Ibn Kathir reminds us, belong equally to the weak and the noble, the poor and the rich.

And beneath it all runs the observation Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws from the grammar itself: even in reproach, Allah preserved His Prophet's ﷺ honour with the third person, and honoured and consoled him with the second.

passages.title: The Reminder on honoured pages by noble scribes
passages.tafsir:
# The Reminder on honoured pages (80:11–16)

After ten ayat of gentle correction over the incident of the blind Companion, the sūrah suddenly turns from the people involved to the revelation itself. These six ayat declare what the Qur'an *is*: a reminder freely offered to whoever wills, whose origin is exalted — written on honoured, purified pages and carried by noble, righteous angel-scribes. What holds the passage together is a single ascending movement: from the message (ayah 11), to the human response it invites (ayah 12), to the celestial pages it rests upon (ayat 13–14), to the hands that carry it (ayat 15–16).

## Why "But no!" — the turning point of the sūrah

Ayah 11 opens with **kallā** — "But no! / Nay". To feel its force you need the scene the sūrah has just described. Ibn Kathir relates from more than one of the scholars of Tafsir that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was in conversation with one of the great leaders of the Quraysh, hoping he would accept Islam, when ʿAbdullah Ibn Umm Maktum — a blind man who had accepted Islam in its earliest days — came urgently beseeching him for guidance. Hoping the Qurayshi leader might be guided, the Prophet ﷺ asked Ibn Umm Maktum to wait, frowned, and turned to the other man. Allah then revealed the opening of the sūrah. Abu Yaʿla and Ibn Jarir both recorded from ʿA'ishah that the sūrah "was revealed about Ibn Umm Maktum, the blind man," who came saying "Guide me" while the Prophet ﷺ was occupied with one of the great leaders of the idolators; Ibn Kathir notes that it appears likewise in Al-Muwatta'.

*Kallā* is the pivot: it closes that episode and corrects the approach behind it. Ibn Kathir explains that Allah here commands His Messenger ﷺ not to single anyone out in conveying the message, but to warn equally the noble and the weak, the poor and the rich, the master and the slave, men and women, young and old — then Allah guides whomever He chooses. The revelation is not a prize to be negotiated with the influential; it is a reminder set before everyone alike.

**What is "it"?** The feminine pronoun in *innahā tadhkirah* ("indeed it is a reminder") is read two ways in the sources, and both converge. Ibn Kathir says it means "this Sūrah, or this advice in conveying knowledge equally among people, whether they are of noble or low class," and he cites Qatadah and As-Suddi, who both said: "This means the Qur'an." Either way, the word **tadhkirah** — "reminder" or "admonition" — is the name Allah gives His revelation here, and it sets the tone for the ayah that follows.

## Ayah 12 — the door left open

"So let whoever wills be mindful of it" (*fa-man shā'a dhakarahu*). This short ayah carries the whole ethic of the passage. Since the message is a reminder, the response is left to human will: no chasing the self-sufficient, no rationing of guidance. Ibn Kathir gives the meaning: whoever wills, remembers Allah in all of his affairs — and he adds that the pronoun *-hu* ("it/Him") could also be understood as referring to the revelation, since the conversation is alluding to it. So the ayah simultaneously reads "whoever wills, let him remember Allah" and "whoever wills, let him take heed of this revelation" — two faces of the same act.

Maʿārif ul Qur'ān, reflecting on the incident behind these ayat, draws from them a standing principle for teachers and preachers: the education and reform of the Muslims takes priority over pursuing those who do not care about faith — "if they do not embrace the faith, there will be no blame on you." The reminder is offered to all; it is forced on no one.

## Ayat 13–14 — the honoured, exalted, purified pages

Having named the Qur'an a reminder, Allah now names where it comes from: "on pages held in honour, highly esteemed, purified" (*fī ṣuḥufin mukarramah, marfūʿah, muṭahharah*).

**Ṣuḥuf** is the plural of *ṣaḥīfah*, "page" or "script." Maʿārif ul Qur'ān explains that the word here refers to the **Lauḥ Maḥfūẓ**, the Preserved Tablet — and answers the obvious question of why a plural is used for a single thing: either because all the divine scriptures are written in it, or because the angels copy their scriptures from it. Ibn Kathir keeps the reference closer at hand — "this Sūrah or this admonition," noting that both meanings are connected, for in reality *all* of the Qur'an is in honoured pages, respected and revered. The two readings are not rivals: what is in the believer's hands below is what stands honoured above.

The three descriptions build on each other:

- **Mukarramah** ("held in honour") — the pages are respected and revered.
- **Marfūʿah** ("exalted") — Ibn Kathir: elevated in status; Maʿārif: exalted *in the sight of Allah*.
- **Muṭahharah** ("purified") — here the two commentaries each contribute something distinct. Ibn Kathir reads it as purity of content: purified "from impurity, additions and deficiency." Maʿārif ul Qur'ān draws the practical, legal sense: it is purified in that those in a state of major ritual impurity (sexual defilement, menstruation, post-natal bleeding) and even minor uncleanness are not permitted to touch it. The pages are pure, so pure hands must handle them — a ruling that flows straight out of the ayah's wording.

## Ayat 15–16 — the hands that carry it

"By the hands of *safarah*, honourable and virtuous." Who are the **safarah**?

Ibn Kathir records that Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid, Ad-Dahhak, and Ibn Zayd all said: "These are the angels." He then cites Al-Bukhari's explanation of why this particular word is used: *safarah* means "ambassadors" — the angels travel around rectifying matters, and when they descend with the revelation of Allah they bring it like the ambassador who rectifies matters between people. The word itself, in other words, casts the angels of revelation as trusted envoys between heaven and earth.

Maʿārif ul Qur'ān opens up the word further: *safarah*, with a fatḥah on the first two letters, may be the plural of *safīr*, meaning a **scribe**. On this reading it refers to the recording angels — or, it adds, to the Prophets (peace be upon them) and those of their aides who write down the revelation; Maʿārif attributes this view to Ibn ʿAbbas and Mujahid. So the word gathers both senses — ambassador and scribe — and the sources record the difference rather than forcing one meaning.

Their description closes the passage: **kirām** ("honourable") and **bararah** ("virtuous, obedient, righteous"). Ibn Kathir explains: they are noble, handsome, and honourable in their creation, and their character and deeds are righteous, pure and perfect. He adds a note on why this description matters: it is necessary for the one who carries the Qur'an — that is, the angel — to be following righteousness and guidance. The hands that bear the revelation down from those purified pages are themselves pure.

## From the Sunnah — joining the noble scribes

The sources seal this passage with a hadith that turns its heavenly imagery into a living promise. Imam Ahmad recorded from ʿA'ishah that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "He who recites the Qur'an proficiently will be with the noble, righteous, ambassador angels (*al-safarah al-kirām al-bararah*), and the one who recites it with difficulty will receive two rewards." Ibn Kathir notes this hadith was reported by the group.

Notice what the Prophet ﷺ did: he took the exact words of ayat 15–16 and made them a rank the believer can attain. The skilled reciter is placed *with* the very angels these ayat describe — and the one who stumbles through the recitation, far from being excluded, earns a double reward for the struggle.

## Living it

Three things follow directly from these ayat as the sources present them. First, guidance is offered, never rationed — the reminder is for "whoever wills," so no seeker is beneath one's attention and no dignitary above needing it. Second, the Book must be met with reverence befitting its origin: honoured pages call for honoured treatment, which Maʿārif ul Qur'ān grounds concretely in the rulings of purity for touching it. Third, the door the hadith opens is for everyone: recite — proficiently if you can, with difficulty if you must — for both paths lead toward the company of the noble and righteous scribes.

passages.title: Ungrateful man and the stages of his creation
passages.tafsir:
This passage is a stern rebuke of the human being who denies the Resurrection — and its method of rebuttal is simply to walk him through his own biography. In seven short ayat, Allah traces the whole arc of a human life: a despised drop, a body shaped in the womb, an eased path into the world, death, the grave, and the raising to come. What binds ayat 17–23 together is a single argument: the One who carried you through every one of these stages unasked has every right over you, and every power to bring you back — yet man, of all creatures, is the one who denies Him. Ibn Kathir titles this whole section "The Refutation against Whoever denies Life after Death."

## "Qutila al-insān" — a curse upon the denier (ayah 17)

The passage opens with words of frightening severity: *qutila al-insānu mā akfarah* — "Condemned are disbelieving humans! How ungrateful they are!" Ad-Dahhak reports from Ibn 'Abbas that *qutila al-insān* means "May man be cursed." Abu Malik said similarly, and added a diagnosis worth sitting with: this refers to "the rejecting type of man, due to his abundant denial without any supporting argument. Rather he denies simply because he thinks it is farfetched and because he lacks knowledge of it." In other words, the denier of resurrection has no case — only incredulity dressed up as certainty.

The second half, *mā akfarah*, carries two shades that the early authorities drew out. Ibn Jurayj said it means "none is worse in disbelief than he is," and Qatadah said "none is more cursed than he is." The word *kufr* itself spans both disbelief and ingratitude, and the passage deliberately plays on both: what follows is a list of favours, so that the denial is exposed not merely as an intellectual error but as rank thanklessness toward a ceaseless Benefactor. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes the flow of the sūrah here: the preceding verses exalted the Qurʼān, a blessing fully appreciated only by people of knowledge — so now the sūrah turns to blessings so bodily and concrete that anyone with basic intellect can grasp them: the favours Allah confers on man from his inception to his end.

## From what was he created? (ayat 18–19)

Allah then asks a question whose answer silences all arrogance: "From what substance did He create them?" Maʿārif ul Qurʼān observes that the question is posed and then answered by the next verse itself, because no other answer is possible: "From a sperm-drop!" The point of this rhetorical structure is to press the humble origin home. Ibn Kathir puts it plainly: Allah explains how He created man "from something despised," and that He who did so "is able to bring him back to life just as He created him initially." A being who began as a *nuṭfah* — a drop of fluid — has no standing to declare his own re-creation impossible.

Then comes *fa-qaddarahu*, and here the scholars found two complementary meanings, both preserved in our sources:

**"He proportioned him."** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that Allah made man with a special design and great wisdom — his stature, body-structure, face, the length and breadth of his limbs, his joints, eyes, nose and ears, all well-proportioned; were any organ to lose its proportion, the face would go awry and every activity would become a problem. The symmetry we take for granted is itself a signature.

**"He decreed for him."** The word *qaddara* comes from *taqdīr*, which is also used for predestination. Read this way, the verse means that while man is still under formation in his mother's womb, Allah predetermines four things for him: his life span, his sustenance, his deeds, and whether he will be miserable or happy. Ibn Kathir gives exactly this explanation, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that it accords with the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud recorded by Shaikhain, as that work cites it. So before the denier ever drew breath, his whole file was already written — by the very Lord he now denies.

## "Then He made the path easy for him" (ayah 20)

On this ayah the early commentators genuinely differed, and Ibn Kathir lays out both views with care.

The first view: *the path* is the birth canal. Al-'Awfi reports from Ibn 'Abbas: "Then He made his coming out of his mother's belly easy for him." This was also the explanation of 'Ikrimah, Ad-Dahhak, Abu Salih, Qatadah, and As-Suddi, and it was the view preferred by Ibn Jarir. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān unfolds the wonder in this reading: Allah forms man in the womb, creation after creation, within three layers of darkness — the belly, the womb, and the amniotic membrane — while the mother herself is unaware of any detail of the process; then, when the child is complete, a body of three to four kilograms passes through an extremely narrow passage, and the mother does not suffer unduly. "So blessed be He Who is the best Creator!"

The second view: *the path* is the path of guidance. Mujahid said the ayah is like Allah's statement, "Verily, We guided him on the path, he is either grateful or ungrateful" (76:3) — meaning, We explained the way to him, clarified it, and made it easy for him to act upon. Al-Hasan and Ibn Zayd said the same, and Ibn Kathir declares: "This is the most correct view, and Allah knows best."

Both readings serve the passage's argument. On the first, the ease of birth is one more unearned favour. On the second, the ayah sharpens the indictment: the road of truth was not hidden from the denier — it was cleared and smoothed for him, and he still refused to walk it.

## Death and the grave — counted among the blessings (ayah 21)

"Then He causes him to die and puts him in his grave." Ibn Kathir notes simply that after creating man, Allah causes him to die and makes him an inhabitant of a grave. But Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws attention to something startling about the placement of this verse: death is mentioned here *in a list of Allah's blessings*. Death, for the believer, is a gift rather than a calamity — the Prophet ﷺ is reported to have expressed it as "the gift of a believer is death" — and there is profound wisdom in death for the order of the whole world.

The word *fa-aqbarahu* — "and put him into the grave" — is itself a favour. When a human being dies, he is not left lying on the earth like other animals, to rot, bloat, and be torn at by scavengers. Even in death he is honoured: his body is washed ceremonially, wrapped in clean cloth, and buried with respect. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a practical ruling drawn from this: the verse indicates that burying the human dead is obligatory. Dignity in death is not a human invention; it is part of how Allah honoured this creature — the same creature who repays Him with denial.

## "Then when He wills, He will resurrect him" (ayah 22)

Here the sequence reaches the very point the denier rejects. Ibn Kathir explains: Allah resurrects man after his death, and this is called *al-baʿth* (resurrection) and *al-nushūr* (resuscitation). Notice the wording of the ayah: *when He wills*. The timing belongs to Allah alone; the certainty of the event does not depend on it feeling near.

Ibn Kathir supports this with parallel verses: "And among His signs is this, that He created you from dust, and then — behold, you are human beings scattered" (30:20), and "And look at the bones, how We bring them together and clothe them with flesh" (2:259). And he cites the hadith in the Two Sahihs, narrated by way of Al-A'mash from Abu Salih, from Abu Hurayrah, that the Prophet ﷺ said: "All of the sons of Adam will decay except for the bone of the coccyx (tailbone). From it he was created, and by it he will be reconstructed." The body that dissolves in the grave is not lost to Allah; the re-creation will proceed from a seed, just as the first creation did.

## "No! He has not done what He commanded him" (ayah 23)

The closing ayah is a sharp *kallā* — "But no!" — and the commentators offered two readings of what exactly has not been done, both recorded by Ibn Kathir.

**Ibn Jarir's reading: man has not fulfilled his duty.** Allah is saying: the matter is not as this disbelieving man claims. He imagines he has discharged Allah's right upon him in his person and his wealth — but "he has not fulfilled for his Lord the obligations that were imposed upon him." On this reading the ayah is the verdict on the whole passage: after every favour listed, from the drop to the grave, man still has not paid what he owes. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads the verse in this spirit: the demand of all these Divine signs and blessings was that man ponder carefully, believe in Allah, and comply with His injunctions — "but the unfortunate creature failed to do so."

**Ibn Kathir's own reading: the resurrection has not yet occurred.** Ibn Kathir writes, "What seems apparent to me of its actual meaning — and Allah knows best —" is that the ayah connects back to "when He wills, He will resurrect him": Allah has *not yet* carried out the resurrection, because the appointed span of humanity's earthly existence has not expired. Allah has decreed mankind's existence and its duration; when that term is complete, He will resurrect His creatures and repeat their creation just as He created them the first time. On this reading, the delay the denier mistakes for refutation is nothing but the unhurried unfolding of a decree.

Both readings stand in the classical tradition, and each answers the denier in its own way — one convicts him of ingratitude, the other dismantles his only "evidence," namely that the resurrection has not happened yet.

## Living with this passage

The sūrah does not leave the argument abstract. Immediately after this passage it turns to something as near as the next meal — "Then let man look at his food" — and Ibn Kathir explains that this is both a call to reflect on Allah's favour and "an evidence in the vegetation's coming to life from the lifeless earth, that the bodies can be brought to life after being decayed bones and scattered dust." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, closing its comment on ayah 23, makes the same turn: having warned man through the signs of his own creation, the sūrah asks him to consider the sources of his food — the water showered from the clouds, the earth cleft with new growth. The proof of resurrection is on your plate every day.

For the believer, this passage asks for two things. First, honest gratitude: every stage it names — your proportioned body, your safe birth, the smoothed path of guidance, even your eventual death and burial — is a favour you never requested and could never repay. Second, urgency: ayah 23 stands as a standing question over every life — *has he done what He commanded him?* The passage warns that the answer, for the heedless, is no — and invites the reader to be among those for whom, before the appointed term expires, the answer becomes yes.

passages.title: Signs in food: rain, grain and orchards
passages.tafsir:
This passage is a single, sustained invitation: *look at your food*. After rebuking the human being who denies the Resurrection (ayat 17–23), the sūrah turns his gaze to something he handles every day — the meal in front of him — and walks him backwards through everything Allah did to put it there: rain poured from the sky, the earth split open, grain, grapes, olives, dates, orchards. What holds ayat 24–32 together is that this one scene does double work: it is a catalogue of favours demanding gratitude, and at the same time a standing proof that the One who brings life out of dead earth can bring bodies out of dead graves.

## Why food, and why here

The placement is deliberate. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that the preceding verses mentioned "the beginning and the end of human life, Divine Omnipotence and Divine blessings," and that the verses now warn the non-believing man: the demand of these Divine Signs and blessings was that he should carefully ponder, believe in Allah, and comply with His injunctions — but the unfortunate creature failed to do so. Now, says the same commentary, come the Divine favours conferred on man *between* the beginning and the end of his life, and so man is asked to consider the sources of his food. Ayah 24 opens with exactly that command: **"Let people then consider their food."**

Ibn Kathir states the double purpose plainly. This verse, he says, is a call to reflect upon Allah's favour — and it also contains an evidence: in the vegetation's coming to life from the lifeless earth is proof that bodies can be brought back to life after becoming decayed bones and scattered dust. The section of his tafsir covering these verses is actually titled "The Growth of the Seed and Other Things is a Proof of Life after Death." In other words, the man who denies the Resurrection because, as Abu Malik put it, "he thinks it is farfetched," is being answered not with an abstract argument but with his own breakfast. He has watched resurrection happen in every field he has ever passed.

## The making of a meal: ayat 25–27

The passage then unfolds the process in order, and every step is Allah's own act — *We* poured, *We* split, *We* caused to grow.

**Ayah 25 — "We pour down rain in abundance."** Ibn Kathir's comment is simple: We sent it down from the sky to the earth. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān likewise: Allah showers down water abundantly from the clouds. The first ingredient of every meal ever eaten falls from above, unearned.

**Ayah 26 — "and meticulously split the earth open."** Ibn Kathir's explanation of this splitting is worth slowing down for: the water settles into the earth, enters into its boundaries, and mingles with the seeds left lying in the soil; from this the seeds grow, rise up, and appear on the surface as vegetation. The "splitting" is that quiet miracle at ground level — dead soil opened from beneath by new growth. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān paints the same picture: at first a fragile shoot germinates and sprouts, and then many different kinds of grain, fruits and gardens come into existence. Something with no strength at all pushes through the earth, because Allah is the one splitting it.

**Ayah 27 — "causing grain to grow in it."** *Ḥabb*, Ibn Kathir notes, refers to all types of seeds and grains.

## The spread of the table: ayat 28–31

Then the catalogue widens, and the early scholars carefully identified each item.

**Grapes and qaḍb (ayah 28).** Grapes, says Ibn Kathir, are well-known. *Qaḍb* is the moist, green herbal plants that animals graze on — also called *al-qat*; this is the explanation of Ibn ʿAbbas, Qatadah, aḍ-Ḍaḥḥak and as-Suddi, while al-Hasan al-Basri said simply, "al-Qaḍb is fodder."

**Olives and date palms (ayah 29).** Ibn Kathir lingers over these two with evident delight in the sheer usefulness Allah packed into them. The olive is a food, and its juice — its oil — is a food too: eaten for breakfast, used as an oil. The date palm's fruit is eaten as *balaḥ*, *busr*, *ruṭab*, *tamr*, *niyāʼ* and *maṭbūkh* — varieties of the date ranging from unripe through ripe to dried in their textures — and its juice is extracted for pulpy fruit drinks and vinegar. One tree, and it feeds you at every stage of its fruit's ripening. The detail itself is the point: reflection on food is not vague; it looks at the actual dates in your hand.

**Ghulb ḥadāʼiq (ayah 30) — dense orchards.** *Ḥadāʼiq* means gardens. On *ghulb*, al-Hasan and Qatadah both said these are gardens of date palms that are thick and handsome; Ibn ʿAbbas and Mujahid said it means everything that is gathered and collected.

**Fruits and herbage (ayah 31).** *Fākihah*, says Ibn Kathir, includes every type of fruit; Ibn ʿAbbas defined it as everything eaten ripe. And *abb* — Ibn ʿAbbas explained — is what the earth grows that is eaten by grazing animals and not people; in another narration from him, "it is the grass for the livestock animals."

## Abu Bakr, ʿUmar, and the word "abb"

That last word, *abb*, occasioned two of the most beloved reports about scholarly humility, and Ibn Kathir records both here.

Abu ʿUbayd al-Qasim bin Sallam reported from Ibrahim at-Taymi that Abu Bakr aṣ-Ṣiddīq was asked about "and fruits and abb," and he answered: "What sky would shade me and what earth would carry me if I said about the Book of Allah that which I did not have knowledge of?" The first man of this ummah after its Prophet ﷺ would rather confess ignorance than guess at Allah's Book.

And Ibn Jarir recorded from Anas that ʿUmar bin al-Khaṭṭab recited Sūrah ʿAbasa, and when he reached "and fruits and abb," he said, "We already know what al-fākihah is, but what is al-abb?" Then he checked himself: "By your life, O Ibn al-Khaṭṭab, this is something overburdensome" — that is, unnecessary to ask about. Ibn Kathir says this report has an authentic chain of narration, transmitted from Anas by more than one person, and he adds an important clarification: ʿUmar was not ignorant of the word's basic meaning. He — and everyone who reads this ayah — knows from Allah's saying "We caused to grow in it..." that *abb* is one of the plants that grows from the earth. What ʿUmar wanted was how it looks, its type, and its exact description — and that, he judged, was something unnecessary to press after.

## "For you and your animals": ayah 32

The passage closes by naming the purpose of the whole spread: **"all as a means of sustenance for you and your animals."** Ibn Kathir explains: a means of livelihood for you all and your cattle in this life *until the coming of the Day of Judgement*. That final phrase quietly re-ties the knot. The table Allah has been setting — rain, grain, orchards — is provision for a journey with a fixed destination. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān observes that having warned man several times about these Divine blessings, the sūrah concludes with the mention of the Resurrection. The meal was never only a meal; it was evidence.

## Living it

What the passage asks for is contained in its first word: *fal-yanẓur* — let him look. Not glance, but consider. Two reflections flow directly from the sources:

- **Gratitude with open eyes.** Every element of the chain — the pouring of the water, the splitting of the earth, the growing of the grain — is attributed to Allah alone. Man's role in the verses is only to eat and to look. The preceding verses cursed the one who took all this and remained ungrateful, denying "simply because he thinks it is farfetched," in Abu Malik's words. Reflection over an ordinary plate of food is this passage's prescribed cure for that ingratitude.
- **The daily proof of Resurrection.** Ibn Kathir's reading turns every field after rain into an answer to the oldest doubt: the earth was dead, water came down, and life rose out of it. The One who does this before your eyes has shown you, in miniature, how He will raise the dead. Whoever truly looks at his food has already seen the Resurrection rehearsed.

passages.title: The Deafening Blast: flight from kin and the two faces
passages.tafsir:
These closing ayat of Sūrah ʿAbasa are a single scene of the Day of Judgement, told in sound, motion, and faces. One deafening cry announces the Day (ayah 33); the bonds people trusted most — brother, mother, father, wife, child — dissolve as everyone flees everyone (34–37); and then the crowd resolves into just two kinds of faces, radiant or dust-covered (38–42). What holds the passage together is a single movement from noise, to flight, to verdict.

## The Deafening Blast (ayah 33)

The passage opens with a word chosen for its violence: *aṣ-ṣākhkhah*. Its root sense is a deafening cry or shout — Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that it refers to the blowing of the Trumpet, which will be a deafening sound. The early authorities cited by Ibn Kathir approached the word from slightly different angles, and it is worth hearing them side by side. Ibn ʿAbbās said, "As-Sakhkhah is one of the names of the Day of Judgement that Allah has magnified and warned His servants of" — for him it is a proper name of the Day itself. Ibn Jarir said, "Perhaps it is a name for the blowing into the Trumpet" — the specific event that opens the Day. And al-Baghawi explained why this word and not another: it is "the thunderous shout of the Day of Judgement," so called "because it will deafen the ears… it pierces the hearing to such an extent that it almost deafens the ears." These readings do not really compete; a sound so overwhelming that it *is* the Day it announces. The Qurʼān does not describe the Blast — it lets the name itself assault the ear.

## Fleeing from the people you love most (ayat 34–36)

What follows is perhaps the most unsettling image in the passage: not fire, not chains, but a man running away from his own family. "On that Day every person will flee from their own siblings, and even their mother and father, and even their spouse and children."

Ibn Kathir explains the mechanism precisely: he will *see* them and then flee from them, and seek to get away from them, "because horror will be so great and the matter will be so weighty." This is not indifference at a distance; it is recognition followed by flight. Qatadah captured the progression: "The most beloved and then the next most beloved, and the closest of kin and then the next closest of kin — due to the terror of that Day."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws attention to something easy to miss in translation: the *order* of the list. In this world a person is normally more anxious about his parents than about his brothers, and more anxious about his wife and children than about his parents. The verse arranges the relationships in exactly that ascending order — brother, then mother and father, then spouse and children — from lower attachment to higher. The rhetorical effect is a tightening screw: even your brother… even your parents… even the wife and children you would die for. In the world, Maʿārif notes, there are relationships that make one willing to lay down his life for the other; on that Day, even if one sees the other standing in front of him, he will turn away. No one will be able to help anyone, despite every natural attachment they shared in this life.

Ibn Kathir sets beside this the famous scene of the intercession, related in an authentic hadith: on that Day each of the great Messengers of firm resolve, when asked to intercede with Allah on behalf of creation, will say, "O myself! O myself! Today I will not ask You concerning anyone but myself." Even ʿĪsā ibn Maryam will say that he will not ask concerning anyone but himself — "I will not even ask Maryam, the woman who gave birth to me." If the Prophets themselves — the best of creation, and the most compassionate — are reduced on that Day to pleading only for their own souls, what of everyone else?

## "Enough concern of their own" (ayah 37)

Ayah 37 states the principle beneath the whole scene: "For then everyone will have enough concern of their own." Ibn Kathir glosses it simply — each person will be so preoccupied with his own case that he is distracted from the affairs of everyone else.

The Sunnah applies this verse in a striking, almost tender exchange. Ibn Abi Hatim recorded from Ibn ʿAbbās that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, "You will all be gathered barefoot, naked, walking and uncircumcised." His wife asked, "O Messenger of Allah! Will we look at or see each other's nakedness?" He ﷺ replied by reciting this very ayah: "Every man among them on that Day will have enough (worries) to make him careless of others" — or he said, "he will be too busy to look." A second narration from Ibn ʿAbbās carries the same question from a woman and the same answer — "O so-and-so woman! Every man among them on that Day will have enough worries to make him careless of others" — and At-Tirmidhi said, "This Hadith is Hasan Sahih." The hadith turns the verse from an abstraction into something you can feel: a terror so total that even shame, one of the most reflexive human instincts, is switched off. No one will be looking at you. Everyone will be looking at their own record.

## The two faces (ayat 38–42)

Then the camera lifts from the fleeing crowd, and the multitude sorts itself into exactly two kinds of faces. Ibn Kathir says plainly: the people will be divided into two parties.

In ayah 38, some faces are *musfirah* — bright. In ayah 39 they are "laughing, rejoicing at good news." Ibn Kathir's comment reverses the direction we might expect: they are happy "due to the joy that will be in their hearts. The good news will be apparent on their faces." The brightness is not cosmetic; it is inner certainty surfacing. These, he says, are the people of Paradise.

In ayat 40–41, other faces carry *ghabarah* — dust — and are overwhelmed by *qatarah*, which Ibn Kathir and Ibn ʿAbbās explain as darkness that covers and overcomes the face. Dust and darkness layered together: the grime of humiliation with gloom settling over it. Where the first faces broadcast good news, these faces broadcast the verdict before it is spoken.

Ayah 42 names them: "those are the disbelievers, the wicked sinners" — *al-kafarah al-fajarah*. Ibn Kathir unpacks the pairing precisely: "disbelievers in their hearts, evildoers in their actions." The two words cover the two dimensions of a human being — inner conviction and outward conduct — and he notes the same pairing elsewhere in the Qurʼān: "And they will beget none but wicked disbelievers" (71:27). Darkness on the face, in the end, is simply what disbelief in the heart and corruption in the deeds look like once nothing can be hidden.

## Why the sūrah ends here

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads this finale as the sūrah's closing warning: those who reject the Qurʼānic message and persist in opposing the Holy Prophet ﷺ will face a day of reckoning when misery, shame and ignominy will be their lot — while the righteous believers will reside in Gardens of Bliss, their faces beaming with joy and happiness. Two parties, and the verdict written permanently on their faces. And between the Blast and the two faces stands the question the passage quietly presses on every reader: on the Day when even your mother cannot claim a moment of your attention, and no one will be able to help you, what will be on *your* face?
